claims.claim: Reviewers describe the gameplay loop as heavily focused on managing a repair shop and answering emails rather than just building PCs.

citations.review_text: This plays much like other similar sim games where you run a storefront and have to answer emails and do jobs troubleshooting and building pcs.  Again, like other simulator games it can be a bit cathartic and relaxing just putting together the PC.  Dragging and dropping the components to each slot.  They do try to get as detailed as you can, but not overly.   I did find it enjoyable enough to scratch that PC building itch.  The storefront simulation side of it is not really my thing and in other simulator games it adds to the gameplay, but I didn’t care too much for it in this title.  Although, without emails asking you to building certain types of PC it wouldn’t be much of a game, so I can and did appreciate it at times.  It’s not as satisfying as say the power washing simulator, but fun enough to pass a little time.  They have been adding a lot of content and DLC I have yet to try, but that looks like they’ve added much more to do.   If simulators are your thing and you’re on Steam, so I’d assume you probably like a nicely built PC then I think if you could get this on sale it’s worth a go.  I’d watch some gameplay videos specifically to see if it seems fun to you as a written review may not do it justice.  I do recommend.
This game is a lot less "PC Building Simulator" and a lot more "Repair Shop Managing Simulator"

Despite the business aspect of running a PC repair shop being quite fun and somewhat engaging, the actual simulation of PC building and diagnostics feels very barebones.

For example, while the interface references "memory channels," these channels aren't physically represented on the motherboard. You can place two DIMMs in any slot and still achieve dual-channel operation, which oversimplifies the process.

At the same time, the game doesn't allow mixing memory modules, despite this being viable in real life with manual memory timings. However, manual timings aren't even a concept in the game, even though it includes an overclocking section in the "BIOS."

I lost interest when I received my first diagnostics mission. I was excited to troubleshoot a system, only to find it booting into a full BIOS with a "No CPU found" status, which completely shattered the immersion.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as lacking a comprehensive tutorial, leaving players to figure out upgrades and hidden requirements largely on their own.

citations.review_text: Neutral review. Definitely has some charm but the game is extremely tedious and tutorial is lacking. If I didn't already have knowledge of PC building I would be lost. The mission system is fun but you're on your own for figuring out "upgrades", otherwise you will buy the wrong part and the game will flag mission as incomplete. This sucks in the beginning because you start out with $0 and you're fighting for every dollar.

As an IT professional in real life, I went into PC Building Simulator expecting a fun “shop management + tech tinkering” experience. Unfortunately, the game ended up being more frustrating than rewarding.

The biggest issue is the hidden checklist system. Jobs don’t complete just because the PC is working, they complete only if you’ve satisfied every obscure trigger the game is secretly tracking. Not missing one tiny thing, but hitting a bug, and you’re stuck with a job that says “Ready to Boot” forever. In real IT, if the PC powers on and the hardware is seated correctly, detected and configured in BIOS, the job is done. Here, the game constantly punishes you for not reading its mind.

The tutorial doesn’t cover these picky requirements either. Instead of teaching you what the game is actually checking for, you only learn by failing contracts and wasting time. It makes the experience feel unfair, not challenging.

And if a contract gets bugged? There’s no debug mode, no console, no way to skip or fix a stuck job. You either abandon it and lose progress, or edit your save file with external tools. That’s unacceptable for a sim-style game that’s supposed to be about shop management and creativity.

I love hard games (Elden Ring, Bloodstained, Project Zomboid, Sons of the Forest), but those games are hard because of design, not because the core systems are broken. PC Building Simulator wastes your time with checklist traps and offers no safety net when they bug out.

Until the devs add proper debug tools, a way to override broken jobs, or at least a more transparent checklist system, I can’t recommend it. It’s a cool idea buried under poor execution.

An incredibly low effort simulator
No voice overs, story, reason to do the job
No real UI or help 
Not really engaging
Won't teach you anything googling the topic wouldnt teach you
Really unclear how to get jobs and can be kind of trial and error to figure it out which is entirely due to a lazy design e.g. the tutorial is separate to the start a new game mode, because they were too lazy to onenct the two parts, and it only teaches you a few things not everything youll need to figure out 

Conclusion: even for $5 this feels like a lazy cash grab

⭐ PC Building Simulator – Review Hours played: 6+

PC Building Simulator is one of those games that sounds niche at first, but once you start tinkering with parts, running diagnostics, and watching your virtual builds come to life, it becomes surprisingly addictive. It captures the satisfaction of building and troubleshooting PCs without the stress (or cost) of real hardware.

What the game does well
Authentic components: Real‑world brands like MSI, Corsair, NZXT, and more make every build feel legit.

Career mode is engaging: Fixing customer PCs, dealing with budgets, and upgrading systems adds a fun puzzle‑solving element.

Great for learning: If you’re new to PC building, this is a safe way to understand how parts fit together and what compatibility looks like.

Relaxing gameplay: There’s something oddly calming about applying thermal paste and cable‑managing a virtual rig.

Where it could improve
Repetition sets in: After a while, many jobs feel similar—clean dust, replace RAM, upgrade GPU, repeat.

Performance quirks: Some animations and UI elements feel a bit clunky compared to the rest of the experience.

Limited challenge: Once you understand the basics, most tasks become straightforward.

Overall
If you enjoy PC hardware, simulation games, or just want a chill experience where you can build dream rigs without spending real money, PC Building Simulator is absolutely worth your time. It’s educational, oddly satisfying, and scratches that tech‑nerd itch. Overall: Recommend

[h2]It's done well, but it's rather dated now. 7/10[/h2]

The game is exactly what it sounds like, only it's a sign of the time it was set in and uses DDR4, mostly HDDs and SSDs and takes ages to unlock a 1080 ti (which seems to be the best GPU available) The expansion adds QOL stuff but I think the pacing is too slow for me to want to play it more than I have.

If you like PC parts and sorts, this game is for you, however the reason why I do not really recommend it at this point is because this game has been succeeded by PC Building Simulator 2, which you should play that over the original due to the fact that there are many more PC parts in that version, not the original.

But if you still like PC parts, by all means you could get this game, which is still somewhat relevant today.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the game serves as an educational and helpful tool for learning basic PC components, assembly, and troubleshooting.

citations.review_text:
Look, we’ve all been there—you want to build a dream rig, but you’re terrified of static electricity or accidentally snapping a motherboard pin. Enter PC Building Simulator.

Honestly? This game is just a total vibe. It’s my go-to "chill out" game. There’s something strangely satisfying about that loop of checking your virtual email, ordering parts, and putting everything together in your workshop. It’s clean, it’s organized, and unlike real life, you don't have to deal with cable management being a total nightmare.

Is it actually educational?
Yes, but let's keep expectations realistic. It’s not going to make you an expert IT tech, and it definitely only scratches the surface of the real-world process. But if you’re a total beginner, it’s genuinely helpful. You’ll walk away knowing exactly how the major components fit together and how they interact. It’s basically "PC Building 101" in a sandbox, which is awesome if you’re prepping for your first real-life build.

The "Infinite Loop" Factor
The replayability here is actually huge. I thought I’d get bored, but I’ve sunk so many hours into this just because it’s fun to mess around with different parts and aesthetics in free-build mode. You don't really get tired of it, unless... well, unless you’re an achievement hunter.

A quick word of warning for my fellow completionists:
If you’re the type who needs that 100% completion badge on your Steam profile—proceed with extreme caution. The grind to get every achievement in this game is not for the weak. It’s a massive, soul-crushing time sink. If you just want to have fun, you'll love it. If you’re coming in to 100% it? Grab a coffee, because you’re going to be here for a long time.

TL;DR:
If you want a fun, casual, educational experience, pick this up. It’s absolutely worth it. Just maybe leave the achievements for the brave souls among us.

I love this game. I wanted to learn how to build a custom computer from basic components. A friend recommended this game and I'm really glad they did. While the game is far simpler than building a computer in real life, it does a great job of teaching what the fundamental parts are, how they fit together, and the basic approach to finding compatible combinations. It even goes into (very over-simplified) methods of tuning and over-clocking your CPU, RAM, and GPU.  And it does it all in a surprisingly fun way, and with components that actually have real-life counterparts.

Fair warning: Any computer you assemble in the game is not guaranteed to work as well (or have the same compatibility) as the real-world analog, so this does not stand in for a part picker. But it was quite amusing to be able to assemble my real-world rig inside the game with the same corresponding parts.

Even once you pass all the story jobs, the game is still enjoyable, as the equipment keeps evolving. The developers regularly add new components as they come to market in the real world, so you can keep building bigger and better desktop rocket ships.

Tips for new players:
* You'll definitely want to invest in any and all screwdriver upgrades as soon as possible. That part of the game gets a little tedious pretty quickly.

* Be prepared for occasional frustration, when a time-constrained job comes in that requires parts you haven't unlocked yet (that only happened to me in the early game).

* Twice I made the mistake of accepting a customer repair/upgrade job on the same day it was due. Since the customer's rig doesn't show up until the next morning, it was an automatic failure. Seems like a bug, tbh, but easily avoidable if you're paying attention.
